hints.content:
Based on the second part of the fundamental theorem of calculus, $g$ is an antiderivative of $f$:

$g'=f$

This table summarizes the relationship between various properties of a function $f$ and its antiderivative $g$:

When the function $f$ is... | The antiderivative $g=\displaystyle\int_a^x f(t)\,dt$ is...
:-: | :-:
Positive $+$ | Increasing $\nearrow$
Negative $-$ | Decreasing $\searrow$
Increasing $\nearrow$ | Concave up $\cup$
Decreasing $\searrow$ | Concave down $\cap$
Changes sign / crosses the $x$-axis | Extremum point
Extremum point | Inflection point

This is an appropriate calculus-based justification for the fact that $g$ is concave up:

$f$ is increasing.

question.content:
This is the graph of $f$.

![Function f is graphed. The x-axis is unnumbered. The graph is a curve. The curve starts on the positive y-axis, moves upward concave up, and ends in quadrant 1.](web+graphie:${☣ LOCALPATH}/images/67077799e9810b29c07d4ad4a3e5400d8d7165cc)

Let $g(x)=\displaystyle\int_0^x f(t)\,dt$.

**What is an appropriate calculus-based justification for the fact that $g$ is concave up?**

[[☃ radio 1]]

choices.clue: When a function is positive, the graph of the antiderivative is increasing, but may be either concave up or down.

Whether the graph of a function is concave down or up doesn't affect whether the graph of the antiderivative is concave down or up. Think about what it means for a function when its antiderivative is concave up.
